In 1972, Brooklyn Tech, [Bronx Science](/wiki/Bronx_Science "Bronx Science"), [Stuyvesant High School](/wiki/Stuyvesant_High_School "Stuyvesant High School"), and [High School for Performing Arts](/wiki/Fiorello_H._LaGuardia_High_School_of_Music_%26_Art_and_Performing_Arts "Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts") become incorporated by the New York State Legislature as specialized high schools of New York City. The act called for a uniform exam to be administered for admission to Brooklyn Tech, Bronx Science, and Stuyvesant. The exam would become known as the [Specialized High Schools Admissions Test](/wiki/Specialized_High_Schools_Admissions_Test "Specialized High Schools Admissions Test") (SHSAT) and tested students in Math and English. With its statewide recognition, the school had to become [co-educational](/wiki/Co-educational "Co-educational"). Previous to this, Brooklyn Tech was All Boys, and had a sister school, [Bay Ridge High School](/wiki/Bay_Ridge_High_School "Bay Ridge High School") which was all girls.[[10]](#cite_note-11)

In 1973, Tech celebrated its 50th anniversary with a dinner-dance at the [Waldorf Astoria](/wiki/Waldorf-Astoria_Hotel "Waldorf-Astoria Hotel"). To further commemorate the anniversary, a [monument](/wiki/Monument "Monument") was erected, with a [time capsule](/wiki/Time_capsule "Time capsule") beneath it, in the north courtyard. The monument has eight panels, each with a unique design representing each of Tech's eight majors at that point.

Malone's statue outside the [Delta Center](/wiki/Delta_Center "Delta Center") (then Vivint Smart Home Arena, pictured in 2017)

Malone is regarded as one of the best power forwards in the history of the NBA and was known as "the Mailman" for his consistent delivery.[[21]](#cite_note-NYT_1988-22) He collected two regular-season MVP Awards, eleven NBA First Team nominations and was also selected to the NBA All-Defensive First Team three times. In 2022, to commemorate the NBA's 75th Anniversary *[The Athletic](/wiki/The_Athletic "The Athletic")* ranked their top 75 players of all time, and named Malone as the 16th greatest player in NBA history.[[61]](#cite_note-62)

Malone wore number 32 for the Utah Jazz. He wore [number 11](/wiki/11_(number) "11 (number)") for the Los Angeles Lakers (number 32 was retired honoring Magic Johnson, though Johnson himself offered to have it unretired for Malone to wear, an offer Malone declined), though he was photographed with a number 32 jersey at his Lakers introductory press conference. Malone also wore number 11 for the Dream Team, as the players wore 4 to 15 to adhere to [FIBA](/wiki/FIBA "FIBA") rules.

Malone has also played 193 playoff games without winning an [NBA championship](/wiki/List_of_NBA_champions "List of NBA champions"), the most in playoff history.[[62]](#cite_note-63)

Lisa Murkowski :: Early life, education, and early career :: chunk_0002
Murkowski was born in [Ketchikan](/wiki/Ketchikan,_Alaska "Ketchikan, Alaska") in the [Territory of Alaska](/wiki/Territory_of_Alaska "Territory of Alaska"), the daughter of Nancy Rena (née Gore) and [Frank Murkowski](/wiki/Frank_Murkowski "Frank Murkowski").[[1]](#cite_note-1) Her paternal great-grandfather was of [Polish](/wiki/Polish_American "Polish American") descent, and her mother's ancestry is [Irish](/wiki/Irish_American "Irish American") and [French Canadian](/wiki/French_Canadian_Americans "French Canadian Americans").[[2]](#cite_note-2) As a child, she and her family moved around the state with her father's job as a banker. After high school, Murkowski interned under Senator [Ted Stevens](/wiki/Ted_Stevens "Ted Stevens") in a Washington summer internship program.[[3]](#cite_note-3) She attended [Willamette University](/wiki/Willamette_University "Willamette University") for two years before transferring to [Georgetown University](/wiki/Georgetown_University "Georgetown University").[[4]](#cite_note-4) She earned a [B.A.](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree in [economics](/wiki/Economics "Economics") from Georgetown University in 1980, the same year her father was elected to the U.S. Senate. She is a member of [Pi Beta Phi](/wiki/Pi_Beta_Phi "Pi Beta Phi") sorority[[5]](#cite_note-Notable_Pi_Phis-5) and represented Alaska as the 1980 Cherry Blossom Princess.[[6]](#cite_note-6) She received her [J.D.](/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") degree in 1985 from [Willamette University College of Law](/wiki/Willamette_University_College_of_Law "Willamette University College of Law").[[7]](#cite_note-7) Murkowski failed the bar exam four times, passing on her fifth attempt.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Murkowski worked as an attorney in the Anchorage District Court Clerk's office from 1987 to 1989.[[10]](#cite_note-2010bar-10) From 1989 to 1998, she was an attorney in private practice in Anchorage. She served on the Mayor's Task Force for the Homeless from 1990 to 1991.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

[Risk factors](/wiki/Risk_factor_(epidemiology) "Risk factor (epidemiology)") for pancreatic adenocarcinoma include:[[2]](#cite_note-NEJM14-2)[[10]](#cite_note-WCR2014-10)[[12]](#cite_note-Bond-Smith-12)[[44]](#cite_note-44)[[45]](#cite_note-45)

* Age, sex, and [ethnicity](/wiki/Ethnic_group "Ethnic group") – the risk of developing pancreatic cancer increases with age. Most cases occur after age 65,[[10]](#cite_note-WCR2014-10) while cases before age 40 are uncommon. The disease is slightly more common in men than in women.[[10]](#cite_note-WCR2014-10) In the United States, it is over 1.5 times more common in [African Americans](/wiki/African_American "African American"), though incidence in Africa is low.[[10]](#cite_note-WCR2014-10)
* [Cigarette smoking](/wiki/Tobacco_smoking "Tobacco smoking") is the best-established avoidable risk factor for pancreatic cancer, approximately doubling risk among long-term smokers, the risk increasing with the number of cigarettes smoked and the years of smoking. The risk declines slowly after [smoking cessation](/wiki/Smoking_cessation "Smoking cessation"), taking some 20 years to return to almost that of nonsmokers.[[46]](#cite_note-46)
* [Obesity](/wiki/Obesity "Obesity") – a [body mass index](/wiki/Body_mass_index "Body mass index") greater than 35 increases [relative risk](/wiki/Relative_risk "Relative risk") by about half.[[12]](#cite_note-Bond-Smith-12)[[47]](#cite_note-47)
* [Radionuclides](/wiki/Radionuclides "Radionuclides") – [Cesium-137](/wiki/Cesium-137 "Cesium-137") and [Iodine-131](/wiki/Iodine-131 "Iodine-131").[[48]](#cite_note-48)[[49]](#cite_note-49)
* Family history – 5–10% of pancreatic cancer cases have an inherited component, where people have a family history of pancreatic cancer.[[2]](#cite_note-NEJM14-2)[[50]](#cite_note-50) The risk escalates greatly if more than one [first-degree relative](/wiki/Consanguinity "Consanguinity") had the disease, and more modestly if they developed it before the age of 50.[[4]](#cite_note-Lancet-4) Most of the [genes](/wiki/Gene "Gene") involved have not been identified.[[2]](#cite_note-NEJM14-2)[[51]](#cite_note-Reznik201

His lectures frequently lasted for three or four hours.[[5]](#cite_note-halford-5) His longest known lecture defined the unit of time known as the "Woodward", after which his other lectures were deemed to be so many "milli-Woodwards" long.[[22]](#cite_note-22) In many of these, he eschewed the use of slides and drew structures by using multicolored chalk. Typically, to begin a lecture, Woodward would arrive and lay out two large white handkerchiefs on the countertop. Upon one would be four or five colors of chalk (new pieces), neatly sorted by color, in a long row. Upon the other handkerchief would be placed an equally impressive row of cigarettes. The previous cigarette would be used to light the next one. His Thursday seminars at Harvard often lasted well into the night. He had a fixation with blue, and many of his suits, his car, and even his parking space were coloured in blue.[[5]](#cite_note-halford-5)

In one of his laboratories, his students hung a large black and white photograph of the master from the ceiling, complete with a large blue "tie" appended. There it hung for some years (early 1970s), until scorched in a minor laboratory fire. He detested exercise, could get along with only a few hours of sleep every night, was a [heavy smoker](/wiki/Chain_smoking "Chain smoking"), and enjoyed Scotch whisky and martinis.[[1]](#cite_note-formemrs-1)[[23]](#cite_note-23)
